sections.text: You chose the Petrov's Defense and achieved comfortable development, but the position quickly became tactical in the center. After 11...Re8, your knight on e4 stepped into a pin on the e-file. When White slipped with 15.Qc2, you found the excellent resource 15...Nb4!, attacking White's queen and forcing the trade of their strong light-squared bishop with 16...Nxd3.

Tension stayed high along the e-file. Your retreat 18...Qe6 created another pin along the e-file against your own knight, but White missed the chance to exploit it with 19.Bd2. You then traded down into a heavy-piece endgame after White grabbed on e4 with 23.Nxe4 fxe4. When White delivered a back rank check with 31.Qb8+, your reply 31...Re8 neutralized the threat.

The game was decided once queens left the board after 37.Qc3 Qxc3. Entering the rook ending a pawn down, you pushed your kingside pawns, but 42...g4 allowed White's king to march into your territory. White collected pawns with 47.Kxg4 and 50.Rxe4, steadily converting their passed pawns until you resigned on move 63.

review.focus: Be careful when placing your queen on the same file as an enemy rook, as seen with 18...Qe6, which pinned your own knight on e4.

review.focus: Watch out for king and queen alignment tactics like 14...Rfe8, which left you vulnerable to knight incursions before White miscalculated.

sections.text: Trouble began when you brought your queen out early with 7.Qd5?, setting up a pin along the diagonal against f7 and g8, as well as a pin down the file against d6 and d8. However, the queen quickly became a target, and Black gained time with 7...Ne7 before you tucked it away on b3. Instead, 7.Qd3 Nf6 would have maintained solid control without exposing your queen.

After trades on f3, Black jumped into the center with 11...Nd4, attacking your queen and your bishop on b5 simultaneously. You needed to drop the queen back to d3 to keep both pieces defended, but you played 12.Qc3?? instead. That allowed 12...Nxb5, losing a bishop outright and prompting your resignation.

review.turning_point: The game was decided instantly on move 12 when 12.Qc3?? failed to defend your bishop on b5, allowing Black to capture it with 12...Nxb5.
review.focus: Be extremely cautious with early queen sorties like 7.Qd5, and when responding to threats against your queen, double-check that your retreat squares don't leave other pieces hanging.

sections.text: You opened aggressively against your opponent's Italian setup, striking in the center with 5.d4. sections.text: You stepped into a Reversed Dragon against the English Opening and started logically by occupying the center with 3...d5 and trading knights on c3. However, you ran into trouble with how you handled your light-squared bishop. After developing with 7...Bg4, you decided on 8...Bxf3, resolving the pin along the d1-f3 diagonal but handing White the bishop pair and an uncontested monster on the long diagonal.

White quickly exploited the open lines. With 10.Rb1, White targeted your b7-pawn. Your choice of 10...Qd7 walked into an immediate loss of material after 11.Rxb7. Instead, 10...Qc8 was needed to keep the b7-pawn guarded and hold your queenside together.

White piled on the pressure with 12.Qa4, creating immense tension against your knight on c6. You needed 12...Nb8 to set up a discovered attack from your queen on d7 against the white queen on a4, but 12...Rfe8 left the knight completely unprotected, allowing 13.Bxc6 where you lost a piece and promptly resigned.

review.turning_point: The decisive break happened on move 10 when 10...Qd7 allowed 11.Rxb7, cracking open your queenside and leaving your knight fatally exposed.
review.focus: Be cautious about giving away the bishop pair needlessly as you did with 8...Bxf3, especially when it leaves the opponent with an unopposed fianchettoed bishop.

The tactics escalated quickly. After 18.Re2 Nd4, you were on the back foot, but Black let you back into the game with 22...f6. Following 24.Qc2 f5, you took control and piled on the pressure, eventually collecting an extra piece with 29.Bxg4 to reach a completely winning position.

review.turning_point: After fighting hard to reach a winning advantage, 33.Rf1 completely overlooked the attack on your queen, handing Black the win on the spot.
review.focus: Always pause to verify what your opponent's move attacks before playing your response, as missing threats like 32...Rc4 can erase an entire game's worth of good work.

sections.text: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, you ran into early opening friction after recapturing 5...cxd6?! and following up with 6...Nc6?. White had chances to seize the center, but instead slipped with 7.Bd3? and 8.Nge2?, which let you trade off White's bishop with 8...Nxd3+! 9.Qxd3.

The game transformed when White chose opposite-side castling with 11.O-O-O?. You immediately mobilized your queenside pawns with 11...b6?!, 13...a5, and 16...b5, creating a direct raceway to White's king.

White tried to strike on the kingside with 17.g4?, but your counter was far faster. You unleashed 17...b4!, creating a discovered attack from your bishop on a6 against the e2-knight. White's position crumbled under the pawn storm, and after 20.Qxb2??, you brought your heavy pieces down the b-file to finish the attack.

review.turning_point: White's overextended 17.g4? gave you the green light to strike with 17...b4!, completely shattering the defense around the white king.
review.focus: Look for central pawn resolutions rather than early knight jumps: resolving tension with 6...dxc4 instead of 6...Nc6? keeps your structure clean.
